html:
The Greek cities of southern Italy and Sicily, which the Romans called Magna Graecia, Great Greece. The map shows them in 400 BCE.

Greeks founded them from the 8th century BCE onward, during the Greek colonisation of the Mediterranean: Cumae near Naples, Syracuse, Taras, Sybaris, Croton, Rhegion and many more. Several grew richer than most cities of Greece itself, with great temples such as those at Paestum and Agrigento. Pythagoras taught at Croton, and the philosophers of the Eleatic school at Elea.

They fought each other and their neighbours, above all Carthage in Sicily, which Syracuse beat at Himera in 480 BCE. Athens' attempt to conquer Syracuse in the Sicilian Expedition ended in disaster in 413 BCE. Around 400 BCE Dionysius I of Syracuse ruled the strongest Greek state in the west. In the 3rd century BCE Rome absorbed them all, after the Pyrrhic War in Italy and the siege of Syracuse, where Archimedes died in 212 BCE.
